sections.body:
Intelligence is the ability to reason, to solve a problem that is not written down in front of you, and to adapt when the situation changes. The second half matters most at work. A procedure you have followed a hundred times is memory, not intelligence. Intelligence is what you do when the manual does not cover the case.

Three words sit next to it, and confusing them causes most of the arguments about people at work. Knowledge is what you have read, seen and stored: the specification of a machine, the rule of a regulation, the history of a customer. Skill is what you can do again and again, reliably, because you have practised it. Intelligence is the capacity that lets you handle the case nobody wrote down. A person can hold a great deal of knowledge and reason poorly, and a beginner can reason well about a machine he has never seen.

Reasoning has two parts that matter. The first is **abstraction**: the ability to take an idea apart from the particular case and see the shape of it. The second is **working memory**: the small amount of information you can hold in mind at one time and still use. A fault on machine A and a fault on machine B look like two problems until somebody sees the common shape, and that step is abstraction. Following a diagnosis with six readings in your head uses working memory, and it runs out faster than most people expect.

No single sentence settles the question, and this article will not pretend that one exists. What follows gives you the words the field uses, the honest state of the research, and a procedure you can run on your own work. Use two of the words carefully. **Expertise** is deep skill and knowledge in one narrow field, built over years of practice. **Aptitude** is the capacity to learn a particular kind of work quickly and well. Neither is the same as general ability, and a person can be excellent at one job and untalented for another.
examples: Intelligence is what lets her work through a procedure she has never seen before.
The manual covers the common case, and the case in front of him was not the common one.
The skill is the routine. The intelligence is what she does when the routine fails.
sections.heading: What intelligence is, and what it is not

terms.example: Intelligence is what lets her find her way through a procedure she has never seen before.
terms.gloss: The ability to reason, to solve a problem that is not written down, and to adapt when the situation changes.

terms.example: Reasoning took her through the fault one step at a time until the cause was clear.
terms.gloss: The work of working out a step-by-step path to an answer, and of checking that path.

terms.example: Abstraction is what let him see that the same fault on two machines had one cause.
terms.gloss: The ability to handle an idea apart from the single case it came from, and to see the shape of it.

terms.example: His working memory filled up with the five readings he was tracking, and he lost the first one.
terms.gloss: The small amount of information a person can hold in mind for a short time and still use.

terms.example: Her expertise on the press line made her the only person who could set the machine up.
terms.gloss: Deep skill and knowledge in one narrow field, built up over years of practice.

terms.example: She had an aptitude for the work: she was accurate within a week of arriving.
terms.gloss: The capacity to learn a particular kind of work quickly and well.

sections.body:
People are not equal across all fields of thinking, and the differences are large enough to notice in the first week of a job. One colleague is fast with words and slow with figures. Another reads a machine layout like a map and gets lost in a long email. A third can hold a conversation with a difficult customer for an hour and cannot find the error in a table of ten columns. A fourth repairs what the others cannot even picture.

One way to talk about this is as a **cognitive profile**: a person has several separate profiles of thinking, and each one has its own strengths and its own limits. The six kinds of thinking used in this article are **verbal reasoning** with words and arguments, **numerical reasoning** with quantity and calculation, **spatial reasoning** with shapes, positions and how parts fit, reading other people, working with patterns and images, and hands-on work with tools and materials.

The idea is not new, and it is not settled science. In the 1980s Howard Gardner proposed a theory of several separate intelligences, and researchers have argued over it ever since: some take the profiles to be real and independent, others see them as different faces of one general ability. The strongest objection is short, and it is worth knowing. When the same people are tested on many different kinds of task, their results tend to move together more than the theory of separate profiles predicts. So treat separate profiles as a useful way of talk and not as a measurement.

That is the honest position, and it is enough for work. A profile does not tell you what a person is worth. It tells you where to put a task. Use the idea in the direction that is safe: describe what somebody is fast at and what they avoid, and put the task where the strength is. Do not use it to measure the value of a person, because that is a step too far and the research does not support it.
examples: My profile is strong with people and weak with long tables of figures.
He reads a layout faster than he reads an email.
The profiles differ and the tasks differ, and that is the whole point of the exercise.
sections.heading: One mind, several profiles

terms.example: Her cognitive profile is strong with people and weak with long tables of numbers.
terms.gloss: The pattern of strengths and weaknesses a person shows across different kinds of thinking.

terms.example: His verbal reasoning was strong: he checked the contract clause by clause and found the gap.
terms.gloss: The ability to follow and build an argument made of words.

terms.example: Numerical reasoning is what she used to compare the two costs before signing.
terms.gloss: The ability to handle quantity, order and calculation.

terms.example: Spatial reasoning is what let him find the leak from a drawing of the pipework.
terms.gloss: The ability to handle shapes, positions and how parts fit together.

sections.body:
The research on this is more careful than the popular versions of it, and the honest picture holds two things at the same time. The first is that different cognitive tests do correlate with each other. A person who scores high on one kind of test tends to score somewhat high on others, even when the tests measure quite different things. This consistent overlap is usually summarised as a **general factor**: a general ability that shows up across many kinds of thinking. The general factor is real, and most researchers accept it.

The second is that the correlations are far from perfect. Two people with the same overall score can have very different profiles, and the difference between those two profiles is often larger than the difference between two people whose overall scores are close. A single number therefore cannot describe a person. It is a summary, and the summary throws away exactly the part that matters when you decide who does which task.

A third piece of evidence is often quoted and often misused: **heritability**. A heritability estimate says how much of the spread of test scores in a population is attributable to genetic differences within that population, in that population's environment. Estimates from different studies and different countries differ widely, and that difference is itself disputed, so no single figure should be repeated as if it were settled. Three things follow from this. A heritability estimate is about the spread inside a group, not about the causes of one person's score. It is not an explanation of why one group of people scores lower than another group. And it describes one population at one time, in the education and health conditions of that time, so it does not say that any difference is permanent.

The practical consequence is calm. What a person has achieved — the **achievement** — depends on ability, but also on practice, instruction, opportunity, health and motivation. That is why the same person can do much better after two years of good training, and why a person who does well on a test today may still do badly on a job nobody has prepared him for.
examples: The general factor is real, and it does not describe anybody by itself.
One score cannot tell me who should do which task.
Heritability is a statement about a group, not about her.
sections.heading: What is general and what is specific

terms.example: The general factor explains why a person who is good on one test is often good on others.
terms.gloss: The general ability that shows up across many different kinds of thinking, usually written g.

terms.example: The heritability estimate for a group of students says nothing about the cause of one student's score.
terms.gloss: The share of the spread of scores inside a population that is attributable to genetic differences within that population.

terms.example: His achievement in the first two years came from long hours and good training, not from a rare ability.
terms.gloss: What a person has actually done, as distinct from what the person could have done.

sections.body:
Work is done in kinds of thinking, and every job is a mix of them. A mechanic needs numbers, space and hands. A recruiter needs people and words. A quality engineer needs patterns and numbers. Knowing which kind a task leans on turns a vague impression into something you can act on.

The last column is the one that matters. A strength in one kind says nothing bad about the other kinds. Read the table as a description of where to put a task, never as a ranking of people.
examples: Give this one to somebody who reads patterns quickly.
This task is mostly words and people, so it does not need the number side.
The last column is not a ranking, and it must not be used as one.
sections.heading: The kinds of thinking and what each one is good for

headers: How to see it at work
rows: The person is quick with words.
It shows how well the person handles meaning and argument.
Ask them to explain a fault to a customer in one paragraph.
It does not mean the person is weak with numbers or with machines.
The person is quick with numbers.
It shows how well the person handles quantity, order and calculation.
Give them a budget, a yield figure or a measurement to check.
It does not mean the person cannot learn numbers, only that they are slower there.
The person is quick with space and mechanics.
It shows how well the person handles shapes, positions and how parts fit together.
Give them a drawing, a layout to plan or a machine to set up.
It does not mean the person is weak in every other kind of thinking.
The person is quick with other people.
It shows how well the person reads other people and works with them.
Give them a customer call, a negotiation or a task that needs an introduction.
It does not mean the person is good at technical work or careful with detail.
The person is quick with patterns and images.
It shows how well the person notices a signal, a trend or a shape inside noise.
Give them a chart, a log with one fault in it or a photo of a damaged part.
It does not mean the person is good at formal proof or at accounting.
The person is quick with hands-on work.
It shows how well the person uses tools, materials and the body.
Give them the machine to service, the sample to measure or the fixture to build.
It does not mean the person cannot do office work or cannot read a document.

sections.body:
A profile is not something you wait to be told. You can build one from real work in an afternoon, and the work you have already done is the best evidence. The six steps are ordered. The first step gathers the evidence, the middle steps test it against other people and against yourself, and the last step turns it into one line you can use.

Two rules keep this honest. Use tasks that really happened, not tasks you would like to have done. And keep the profile about kinds of thinking, not about rank or pay, because the moment it becomes a ranking, the people you ask stop answering honestly.
examples: Write down five tasks you did well and were trusted with.
Ask two people what I am fastest at, and what they would not give me.
Strong at people, weak at figures; now test it on the next real job.
sections.heading: How to find your own profile at work
steps: Collect the tasks you did well and were trusted with. Write down five or six real tasks from the last year where the result was good and you were asked to do it again. Write what the task was, not how clever you think you were.
Ask two people who have seen your work. Give each one the same two questions: what am I fastest at, and what would you not give me? Compare the two answers and keep what appears in both.
Name the task where you were slowest, and say why. Write the reason next to it: too many steps, the wrong tool, missing information, not enough time. The reason decides what you do next.
Try the opposite kind of task once. Take one task of the kind you avoid, give yourself time to prepare, and write down in three lines what happened.
Check what other people find hard about the same task. Ask somebody who is good at it what is difficult in it. If the difficulty is not the one you assumed, your profile is wrong and needs changing.
Write the profile in one line and test it on a real job. One line: strong at X, weak at Y, strong at Z. Then apply it to the next real task you get, and correct the line if the task says otherwise.

sections.body:
This article describes a way of thinking about ability. It does not rank people. A profile says where a person is fast; it does not say how much a person is worth, and it must not be used as a ranking in a team, a class or a hiring list.

It does not diagnose anybody. Real problems with reading, with number sense or with attention are clinical questions, and they need a qualified professional who can test and describe them properly. This article cannot do that, and a profile you built yourself is not a diagnosis.

It does not replace a professional assessment, and it does not predict how somebody will do a job. A test result is a sample taken on one day, under one set of conditions. A job is months of work in a real setting with other people, and the two are not the same thing. Use this article to ask better questions and to give better words to the answers you already have.
examples: This article gives the words, not a diagnosis.
A profile is not a ranking, and I will not use it as one.
The assessment is the professional's job; this is only the vocabulary.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
These are the sentences for a review, a handover or a planning meeting. They name the kind of thinking a task needs, and they keep the difference between ability and fit clear. None of them ranks anybody.

The first four are for your own work. The last four are for when you hand a task to somebody else.
examples: This task is more about the people than about the numbers, and I am faster on the people side.
I am slow with tables of figures, so give me the summary and I will check the source.
His strength is spatial: he reads a layout faster than he reads a report.
She is not slow; the task is simply not the kind she is strongest in.
This needs the pattern reading, and that is not my line, so let us give it to somebody who reads signals quickly.
The strengths of the team are spread well: the numbers, the people and the machines are covered.
I am not the fastest here, but I know this system, so I will check the result before we use it.
Let us match the task to the strength instead of asking one person to do everything.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use about ability and fit

sections.body:
One person cannot be strong in every kind of thinking at once, and a team is not a smaller version of one strong person. A team is faster when the strengths are spread across its members, and slower when the same kind of thinking is expected from everybody. The practical move is not to find the best person. It is to put each task with the person whose profile fits it.

Telling somebody that a task does not fit their profile needs the right words. Say what the task needs, say that you are asking because of that, and say that you are not making a judgement about their ability. *"This one is mostly about reading patterns in a noisy log, and that is not where I am strongest, so I would rather ask somebody who reads signals quickly. On the rest of the report I need your judgement."* An **analogy** from the other person's own field often does the job better than any explanation of your own field: a control room and a cockpit are both places where a few signals matter more than the hundred others.

There is a second reason to spread the strengths. The team sees what one person cannot. When the same kind of thinking does every check, the team inherits the same blind spot. A colleague who thinks in a different way finds the fault the rest of you were not looking for, and finding it is not luck. It is the point of having the other mind in the room.

A hiring decision that ignores the profile wastes people, and it usually wastes them quietly. The wrong person takes the job, works hard, and does not reach the result; the manager concludes that the person is weak, when the real problem was the fit. The fix is not a better test. It is a job description that names the kind of thinking the work needs, so that applicants can be compared on the right thing, and so that the person who is hired can grow into the work instead of being measured against it forever.
examples: This task needs the pattern reading, so let us give it to the person who does that fastest.
Our strengths are spread across the team, and that is why we are faster than one strong person.
It is not a judgement about your ability; it is about what the task needs.
sections.heading: How a team of different minds works

terms.example: The analogy he used, a control room and a cockpit, made the new system easy to explain.
terms.gloss: A comparison with something similar that helps explain an unfamiliar thing.

item.summary: Intelligence is not one number, and it is not the same as knowledge or skill. After reading this you can describe what intelligence is, explain why one mind is strong in one field and weak in another, separate the general factor from the specific profiles, and use six steps to write your own profile and put it to work in a team.
item.title: The Nature of Intelligence: Why One Mind Shines in One Field
